chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Turning down the offer to lead a Cotton Club band; the super sideman
summary: About 1939 Freddie Jenkins proposed a relief band at the Cotton Club, but Jackson chose to remain a sideman.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: No, but I was offered one. In fact they told me I could have one in the Cotton Club when they moved downtown. Now Duke was in there at the time, and Freddie Jenkins, he had talked to Herman Stark and them. He said, "Why don't you get a band together and we'll put you in as the relief band?"

So Fred Jenkins was around New York at the time, so I said, "No, I don't want to be bothered with a band." I had seen what other band leaders went through and I wanted just to keep my mind on playing and singing. And I didn't -- You know, to keep a bunch of guys working and keep them happy and satisfied, that was a job in itself, --

And I love my friends and I wanted to keep all my friends, so I said the best way to do that is not to become a band leader. I'd rather play for somebody else and play with somebody else and enjoy that, which I did.
Yeah. That is one of the reasons we call you a super sideman. You, an instrumentalist, have played for all of the greats and made all of these great
musicians, these great band leaders, helped them to perform great orchestras. So this -- I just want to specifically say -- this is why we consider you the super sideman.
